newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish equity market seen up 6 pct by June 97-broker.
newsitem.headline: Irish equity market seen up 6 pct by June 97-broker.

text.p: The Irish equity market is in strong shape and the ISEQ equity index could notch up another six percent by June 1997, NCB stockbrokers said on Wednesday.
"Our June 1997 target for the ISEQ is 2850, up six percent from current levels," NCB said at a news conference after the release of its Irish Equity Market 1997 Outlook.
NCB head of research John Conroy warned however that key U.S. and UK equity markets were likely to restrain overall performance over the next three to six months.

"In the U.S. the general backdrop for equities remains positive for the medium term," Conroy said. "However, the pace of recent gains leaves the market vulnerable to setbacks in the bond market over the coming months."
In Britain, NCB said equity market valuations were low by international standards but the economic policy mix gave rise for concern.
NCB felt with the UK economy on a recovery path, the preferable strategy would be to tighten fiscal rather than monetary policy, thus allowing the exchange rate to stabilise or drift back.
The brokers remain positive on Ireland.
"The Irish economic story remains compelling," NCB said. "Real GNP growth should again be over five percent in 1997 and inflation should remain below 2.5 percent."
It said economic growth also benefited from favourable current demographic trends.
On the equity market it said earnings revisions were more likely to be upwards although valuation gaps between the leading companies and their benchmark sectors overseas had narrowed.
They said there was also upside potential from acquisition development and from takeover activity or speculation.
Looking further ahead NCB said the single most important factor for the Irish equity market would be European Monetary Union (EMU), which it felt confident would become a reality in January 1999.
It expected the challenges presented by EMU to be many and varied.

On the plus side NCB expect Irish interest rates to fall as they converge with German rates and exposure to sterling depreciation, assuming the UK stays outside EMU, to be less than is currently feared.

NCB felt that if there was a serious political downside risk to being part of EMU it was more likely to reside in the constraints that EMU would impose, some of which would be the limited room to respond to economic shocks that affect Ireland disproportionately.
In the medium term, technical factors relating to funds flows may be of greater importance, it said.

"Put simply, Irish pension funds are likely to be restructured to reflect the absence of exchange risk," NCB said. "The absence of a requirement to match local liabilities with local asset is likely to result in a higher proportion of asset in non-Irish issues."

It said the size of the reduction in funds in Irish equities is hard to predict but it guessed weigthings could fall to 15-20 percent from a current 23 percent over the next few years with the risk of more on the downside.
